messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv is a thirty-nine-year-old interior designer living with his wife in a suburban Boston neighborhood. Two years ago, his younger brother, Anil, died suddenly in a car accident on the way home from a late shift. Rajiv received the call at his studio and drove to the hospital, but Anil was already gone. What Rajiv remembers most vividly from that night is the fluorescent light in the waiting room, the way it flickered, and the nurse’s voice saying something he could not quite grasp. In the months that followed, he could not enter the hospital wing where it happened, and he stopped driving past the intersection where the accident occurred. His work, which had once been a source of pride, became a minefield. A client casually mentioned that her mother had recently passed away, and Rajiv felt his chest tighten and his palms go slick; he excused himself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink until his breathing slowed. He had come to believe that if he could imagine the worst thing that might happen in any given situation, he would somehow be ready for it, and so he began mentally rehearsing catastrophic outcomes before meetings, before driving, before his wife left for work. What frightened him most was the way his body reacted before his mind could catch up—a sudden jolt of heat, a racing heart, a sense that the world had tilted—and those episodes left him irritable for hours afterward, snapping at colleagues or withdrawing from conversation entirely. Anniversaries of the death were unbearable; the week before the two-year mark, he told his wife he had to work late every night, and he avoided the family WhatsApp group where relatives were already sharing photos. He also refused to attend any funeral, even for distant acquaintances, because the sight of a casket or the smell of flowers sent him into a state where he felt as though he was back in that waiting room, the fluorescent light flickering above him. The worst-case rehearsal, which he initially believed was protective, only made the feeling of imminent danger more constant. At a project site last month, a contractor joked about a near-miss on the highway, and Rajiv’s mind instantly spun out a detailed scene of the crash taking his brother; his hands shook, and he had to sit down. His wife had started to notice that he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind, and that he slept poorly the nights before any date that held personal significance. What finally brought him to seek help was an outburst at a team meeting—he had shouted at a junior designer for rearranging a sample board, and afterward he could not explain why he had been so angry. He sat in his car in the parking lot afterward, his heart pounding, and realized that the rehearsal had not prepared him for anything; it had only made the world feel more dangerous. He is terrified that he is losing control, that the irritability and the flashbacks are pushing away the people he loves, and he is hoping that talking to someone might help him stop the cycle before it costs him his marriage and his career.
